title: Related or not? Development of spontaneous Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in a patient with chronic, well-controlled HIV: A case report and review of the literature
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with long-standing, well-controlled HIV infection, hepatitis B, hypertension, and peripheral vascular disease presented with 3 months of progressive subacute neurocognitive decline. His symptoms included conceptual apraxia, apathy, memory impairment, and gait disturbance, initially attributed to “pseudo-dementia” and polypharmacy. His symptoms worsened despite medication adjustments and culminated in admission for altered mental status and aspiration pneumonia.

On transfer, he appeared cachectic and chronically ill. Temperature was 101.2°F, blood pressure 140/82 mm Hg, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. He was minimally interactive and mute but followed simple commands. Cranial nerves were intact. Motor examination showed increased tone in all extremities with atrophic bulk, bilateral upper-extremity clonus, and hyperreflexia (3+ at biceps and brachioradialis); lower-extremity reflexes were absent.

Laboratory studies revealed new pancytopenia (white blood cell count 1.4 ×10^9/L; hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL; platelets 64 ×10^9/L), thought secondary to sepsis. His serum sodium was 152 mmol/L and corrected with free water without mentation change. One month earlier, CD4 count was 531/µL and HIV-1 RNA was undetectable.

A lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 16 cm H2O, protein 59 mg/dL, glucose 56 mg/dL, and no cells. CSF studies for Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, and cytomegalovirus PCR; VDRL; cryptococcal and Histoplasma antigens; bacterial and fungal cultures; and JC virus PCR were all negative.

Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated prominent diffusion restriction in the bilateral caudate, putamen, and thalami, as well as gyriform cortical restricted diffusion in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres. Continuous EEG monitoring revealed diffuse slowing without seizures or periodic discharges.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. HIV-associated neurocognitive decline was considered but deemed unlikely — “his HIV was well controlled, with a CD4 count >400/µL, and an undetectable viral load for most of the last 15 years made this less likely.”  
2. A subacute to chronic CNS infection was ruled out — “these CSF studies were unremarkable.”  
3. Structural brain lesions were excluded despite diffusion abnormalities — “Brain imaging revealed no clear structural lesion, but did show a peculiar pattern of diffusion restriction…”  
4. Nonprion causes of diffusion restriction were excluded — “Such findings are non-specific and can be seen in a variety of disease processes… All of these conditions except prion diseases were excluded based on laboratory work-up and clinical phenotype.”  
5. Other rapidly progressive dementias were considered less likely given the tempo — “Even with the most rapidly progressive dementias, virtually none result in the death of the patient within weeks to months of symptom onset. The latter is more typical of CJD.”
